name: Iraq

summary.text: Iraq is a republic in the Middle East, governed by Saddam Hussein from 1979 until the U.S.-led invasion of March 2003. The stated basis for the invasion was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction and had ties to al Qaeda. The Iraq Survey Group's 2004 Duelfer report found that Iraq had ended its nuclear program and destroyed its chemical stockpile in 1991 and had no active WMD programs at the time of the invasion. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence found in July 2004 that most key judgments of the October 2002 National Intelligence Estimate were overstated or unsupported, and in June 2008 that some prewar statements by senior officials, including claims of an Iraq-al Qaeda partnership, were not substantiated by the intelligence. The UK's Iraq Inquiry (Chilcot) reported in July 2016 that judgments about Iraq's WMD had been presented with a certainty that was not justified.

facts.claim: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's July 9, 2004 report on prewar intelligence on Iraq concluded that most of the major key judgments in the October 2002 National Intelligence Estimate, Iraq's Continuing Programs for Weapons of Mass Destruction, either overstated or were not supported by the underlying intelligence reporting. The committee also found that the intelligence community had been right in finding no link between Iraq and al Qaeda.
facts.quote: most of the major key judgments either overstated, or were not supported by, the underlying intelligence reporting.

facts.claim: The Iraq Survey Group's Comprehensive Report (the Duelfer report, September 30, 2004) found that Saddam Hussein ended Iraq's nuclear program in 1991 after the Gulf War and that there was no evidence of concerted efforts to restart it; that Iraq unilaterally destroyed its undeclared chemical weapons stockpile in 1991 with no credible indications that production of chemical munitions resumed; and that there was no evidence that after 1995 Iraq planned to resume biological weapons production. It also found that Saddam intended to preserve the capability to reconstitute WMD once sanctions were lifted.
facts.quote: Saddam Husayn ended the nuclear program in 1991 following the Gulf war. ISG found no evidence to suggest concerted efforts to restart the program.

facts.claim: The 9/11 Commission reported in 2004 that contacts between Iraq and al Qaeda, including a 1994 meeting with an Iraqi intelligence officer, did not appear to have resulted in a collaborative relationship, and that it had no credible evidence that Iraq and al Qaeda cooperated on attacks against the United States. It also concluded that the alleged April 2001 meeting in Prague between Mohamed Atta and an Iraqi intelligence officer did not occur, citing evidence that Atta was in the United States at the time.
facts.quote: We have no credible evidence that Iraq and al-Qaida cooperated on attacks against the United States.

facts.claim: On June 5, 2008 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released its Phase II report on whether public statements about Iraq by U.S. officials were substantiated by intelligence (S. Rept. 110-345), approved 10-5. It concluded that statements and implications by the President and Secretary of State suggesting that Iraq and al Qaeda had a partnership, or that Iraq had provided al Qaeda with weapons training, were not substantiated by the intelligence, and that the Vice President's description of the alleged Prague meeting between Mohamed Atta and an Iraqi intelligence officer as pretty well confirmed was not substantiated by the intelligence at the time.
facts.quote: statements and implications by the President and Secretary of State suggesting that Iraq and al-Qa'ida had a partnership, or that Iraq had provided al-Qa'ida with weapons training, were not substantiated by the intelligence

facts.claim: The same June 2008 Senate Intelligence Committee report found that many prewar statements on Iraq's weapons were generally substantiated by the intelligence then available, but that officials often did not convey the level of dissent or uncertainty within the intelligence agencies; for example, some agencies supported the claim that Iraq was seeking nuclear weapons while others could not substantiate it. Chairman Jay Rockefeller said the administration repeatedly presented intelligence as fact when in reality it was unsubstantiated, contradicted, or even non-existent; Vice Chairman Christopher Bond and the White House rejected the report's framing.
facts.quote: intelligence substantiated most of the administration's statements about Iraq before the war. But officials often did not mention the level of dissension or uncertainty in the intelligence agencies about the information.

facts.claim: The UK Iraq Inquiry (Chilcot report), published July 6, 2016, concluded that the judgements about the severity of the threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction were presented with a certainty that was not justified; that the Joint Intelligence Committee should have made clear to Prime Minister Blair that the intelligence had not established beyond doubt that Iraq was still producing chemical and biological weapons or pursuing nuclear weapons; and that the UK joined the invasion before peaceful options for disarmament were exhausted, so military action was not a last resort. It found no evidence that intelligence was improperly included in the September 2002 dossier.
facts.quote: The judgements about the severity of the threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction – WMD – were presented with a certainty that was not justified.

facts.claim: The Sunday Times published on May 1, 2005 a memo recording a July 23, 2002 meeting of Prime Minister Tony Blair and senior advisers, in which the head of MI6, Sir Richard Dearlove, reported after a visit to Washington that military action was now seen as inevitable and that the intelligence and facts were being fixed around the policy.
facts.quote: the intelligence and facts were being fixed around the policy

facts.quote: Simply stated, there is no doubt that Saddam Hussein now has weapons of mass destruction.

facts.claim: The Center for Public Integrity's January 2008 study, Iraq: The War Card, counted 935 false statements about the threat from Iraq made by eight senior Bush administration officials between September 11, 2001 and September 11, 2003, including 260 by President Bush (232 on WMD and 28 on al Qaeda links) and 254 by Secretary Powell, and characterized them as part of an orchestrated campaign.
facts.quote: part of an orchestrated campaign that effectively galvanized public opinion and, in the process, led the nation to war under decidedly false pretenses

openQuestions: The site's framing that 9/11 was misattributed in order to start an endless war is not what these sources show. They show (a) official findings that the stated WMD and al Qaeda bases for the invasion were overstated, unsupported or, after the fact, wrong (SSCI 2004 and 2008, Duelfer 2004, Chilcot 2016), and (b) the Downing Street memo's report that the intelligence was being fixed around the policy. None of the official inquiries finds that officials knew the claims were false, and none links the Iraq decision to any finding about Saudi Arabia. The 9/11 Commission and SSCI both found no Iraq-al Qaeda operational link.

The Sunday Times' original May 1, 2005 publication of the Downing Street memo was not retrieved; the item is sourced to a mirrored news report and a Carnegie Endowment commentary. The owner should replace these with the Sunday Times page if available. Blair's confirmation of the memo's authenticity was reported only by a party press release and was not recorded.

The 2008 SSCI conclusions are quoted from the committee's press release and news coverage; the GovInfo PDF of S. Rept. 110-345 is cited for the full text and should be checked for exact wording of each numbered conclusion, including which WMD statements were found 'generally substantiated'.
The Chilcot executive summary paragraph numbers and the 'not a last resort' wording come from the House of Commons Library briefing and Hansard rather than the PDF itself.
The Center for Public Integrity's per-official counts for Cheney (48) and others came from a single secondary summary and were left out except the Bush and Powell totals, which two sources agreed on.

The site's consent page cites a Financial Times figure of $39.5 billion in Iraq contracts to KBR; that figure was not researched here and halliburton.json records the House minority staff's 2004 figures instead.
